changed.was: Monks of the priory of Saint-Vivant held vines on this slope in the Middle Ages, and by the seventeenth century the vineyard was known as La Romanée. In 1760 it was bought by Louis François de Bourbon, Prince de Conti (1717 to 1776), who outbid, the story goes, Madame de Pompadour (1721 to 1764), and who kept its wine, as it is told, for his own table; the vineyard came to carry his name. The Revolution took it from his heir and sold it at auction as national property. In 1869 it was bought by a Burgundian landowner whose heirs, the de Villaine family among them, built the domaine around it, and in 1933 the domaine added La Tâche, its second monopole. In 1942 the Leroy family bought into the domaine, which the two families have run together since as a société civile. Romanée-Conti kept its ungrafted vines through phylloxera until the harvest of 1945; they were pulled up, the vineyard was replanted in 1947, and it made no wine again until the early 1950s. For a sommelier it is the name every guest knows and few have tasted: a grand cru held whole by one domaine, light and endless rather than powerful.
changed.now: The priory of Saint-Vivant held this vineyard in the Middle Ages, and by the middle of the seventeenth century it was known as La Romanée, for a reason nobody has found. In 1760 it was bought by Louis François de Bourbon, Prince de Conti (1717 to 1776), and the vineyard came to carry his name; the tale that he outbid the King's favourite for it is doubted. The Revolution seized it from his son, and in 1794 it was sold at auction. In 1869 it was bought by a wine merchant whose heirs, the de Villaine family among them, built the domaine around it, and in 1933 the domaine bought the rest of La Tâche at the auction of the Liger-Belair estate, which made it a second monopole. In 1942 the domaine became a société civile, and the Leroy family bought half of it. Romanée-Conti kept its ungrafted vines through phylloxera until the harvest of 1945; they were then pulled up, the vineyard was replanted in 1947, and the next Romanée-Conti was the 1952 vintage. For a sommelier it is the name every guest knows and few have tasted: a grand cru held whole by one domaine, light and endless rather than powerful.
changed.why: The priory and the name La Romanée by about 1651, its reason unknown (Wikipedia, Decanter, Fine and Rare, Beaune Tourism); the Prince de Conti's dates (Wikipedia, Sotheby's); the Pompadour rivalry called a myth by Wikipedia; seized from his son and auctioned in 1794 (Wikipedia, Sotheby's); a merchant in 1869 whose heirs include the de Villaines (Justerini and Brooks, Berry Bros and Rudd); the rest of La Tâche bought at the Liger-Belair auction of 1933 (Vinous, Sotheby's); the société civile of 1942 and the Leroy half (Justerini and Brooks, Berry Bros and Rudd); replanted in 1947 and next made in 1952 (Wikipedia, Vinous).

changed.was: Gevrey's great vineyard began with its neighbour: the monks of the abbey of Bèze planted Clos de Bèze in the seventh century, and Chambertin, the story goes, is the field of a peasant named Bertin who planted beside them, the champ de Bertin. By the eighteenth century its wine was famous far beyond Burgundy, and Napoleon, as the legend tells it, drank it at his campaigns, cut with water. In 1847 the village of Gevrey added the vineyard's name to its own. Armand Rousseau (1884 to 1959) inherited a few vines in the village at the start of the twentieth century and built the domaine by marriage and purchase, adding parcels of the grands crus. In the 1930s, urged on by a Paris wine writer, he began to bottle his own wine and sell it under his name, among the first growers of the Côte d'Or to do so, when most sold their wine in cask to the merchants of Beaune and Nuits. His son Charles (1923 to 2016) took over in 1959 and widened the holdings. Chambertin, firmer and slower than the house's Clos de Bèze, shows the domaine's method plainest: destemmed fruit, new oak kept for the grands crus, and patience.
changed.now: Gevrey's great vineyard began with its neighbour: in 640, as the Bourgogne wine body records it, a duke gave a clos here to the monks of the abbey of Bèze, and Chambertin, the story goes, is the field of a man named Bertin who planted beside them, the champ de Bertin, a name in the records by the thirteenth century. Napoleon, as the legend tells it, drank its wine with water at his meals. In 1847 the village of Gevrey added the vineyard's name to its own. Armand Rousseau (1884 to 1959) came into a house and his first vines in Gevrey with his marriage in 1909, and he bought parcels of the grands crus, Mazis-Chambertin in 1937 among them. In the 1930s, urged on by the editor of the Revue du Vin de France, he began to bottle and sell his own wine, among the first growers of the Côte d'Or to do so, when most sold their wine in cask to the merchants. His son Charles, who died in 2016, took charge in 1959 and widened the holdings. Chambertin, firmer and slower than the house's Clos de Bèze, shows the domaine's method plainest: every barrel new, and patience.

Bonnes-Mares is the domaine's largest grand cru holding, and it shows the house plainly, because the wine is drawn from both the red clay and the pale marl of the cru. changed.was: In 1141 the nuns of Notre-Dame de Tart, a Cistercian house, acquired the vineyard on the slope of Morey and gave it their name. They held it for six and a half centuries, and in all that time it was never divided. The Revolution took it from them, and in 1791 it was sold at auction as national property to the Marey-Monge family, who kept it whole for more than a century. In 1932 it passed to the Mommessin family, merchants of the Mâconnais, and when the appellations of the Côte de Nuits were drawn it was ranked a grand cru in its own right.
